entry: Country in the Caucasus region, between Eastern Europe and West Asia. It borders the [[Black Sea]] to the west and [[Russia]] to the north, and most of its 3.9 million people are ethnic Georgians; over a third live in the capital, [[Tbilisi]]. Known for the world's earliest known winemaking sites, Georgia adopted Christianity in the early 4th century and was unified under the Kingdom of Georgia, which reached its Golden Age in the High Middle Ages. The [[Russian Empire]] gradually annexed the country from 1801. After brief independence following the Russian Revolution, the Red Army annexed Georgia in 1921, and it became a republic of the [[Soviet Union]] until seceding in April 1991. After the 2003 Rose Revolution, Georgia pursued integration with the [[European Union]] and [[NATO]], worsening relations with Russia and culminating in the [[Russo-Georgian War]] of 2008. It is a unitary parliamentary republic and became the second country to legalize cannabis in 2018.

Official language of [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] and the most widely spoken of the Kartvelian languages. It has about 3.8 million speakers, is the native language of most Georgians, and serves as a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] for speakers of related languages. It is not related to any of the world's major [[Language family|language families]] found outside Georgia; its closest relatives are Mingrelian and Laz, with Svan more distant. Written in its own unique scripts, of which Mkhedruli is dominant in modern use, it is agglutinative, has seven noun cases, and uses a vigesimal numeral system based on 20.

Soviet military leader. A peasant's son from near [[Moscow]], he served in World War I and then the [[Red Army]] in the [[Russian Civil War]]. He won a decisive victory over Japanese forces at Khalkhin Gol in 1939 and became chief of the General Staff in 1941, but lost the post after disagreeing with [[Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] over the defense of Kiev. He later fought at Stalingrad and Kursk and was promoted to Marshal of the Soviet Union in 1943. In 1945 he commanded the 1st Belorussian Front in the [[Battle of Berlin]], accepted the German surrender, and became the first military governor of the Soviet occupation zone. Stalin then saw him as a potential threat and gave him minor commands. After Stalin's death, Zhukov backed [[Nikita Khrushchev]] and became defense minister in 1955, but was forced to retire in 1957.

Circular orbit above Earth's equator, following the direction of Earth's rotation. A satellite in it has an orbital period equal to Earth's rotational period, one sidereal day, so it appears motionless to ground observers. The orbit lies at an altitude of 35,786 km (22,236 mi) and is a special case of [[Geosynchronous orbit|geosynchronous orbit]]. The concept was popularized by [[Arthur C. Clarke]] in a 1945 paper as a way to revolutionize telecommunications. [[Communications satellite|Communications satellites]] use it so that ground antennas can point permanently at them without moving, and weather and navigation satellites also operate there. Satellites are launched into a temporary orbit and placed in a "slot" above a fixed point on Earth's surface, then require periodic station-keeping. Retired satellites are moved to a higher graveyard orbit to avoid collisions.

Earth-centered orbit with a period matching Earth's rotation. Its period is one sidereal day, 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds, so an observer on the surface sees the object return to the same position in the sky each day. Its path may stay still or trace a figure-eight, depending on inclination and eccentricity. A circular geosynchronous orbit has a constant altitude of 35,786 km (22,236 mi). The [[Geostationary orbit|geostationary orbit]] is a special case, circular and in the equatorial plane, with both inclination and eccentricity equal to 0. Communications satellites are often placed in geostationary or near-geostationary orbits so that their antennas need not move. In a 1945 paper, [[Arthur C. Clarke]] popularized the concept as a means of relaying communications; the collection of satellites in this orbit is called the Clarke Belt.

Electricity generated from geothermal energy. Technologies include dry steam, flash steam and binary cycle [[Power station|power stations]]; 32 countries had operational geothermal stations as of 2022. Worldwide capacity was 15.4 gigawatts (GW) in 2019, of which 23.9% (3.68 GW) was in the [[United States]]. The world's first commercial geothermal power station was built in 1911 at Larderello, Italy, and the first successful U.S. station began operating at The Geysers in [[California]] in 1960. A binary cycle station was first demonstrated in the [[Soviet Union]] in 1967. Because heat extraction is small compared with Earth's heat content, geothermal power is considered sustainable and [[Renewable energy|renewable]]. Its emissions average 45 grams of [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] per kilowatt-hour, less than 5% of those of coal-fired plants. The Geothermal Energy Association estimates that only 6.9% of global potential has been tapped.

38th president of the United States (1974–1977). A Michigan Republican in the House of Representatives for nearly 25 years, he became vice president in December 1973 after Spiro Agnew resigned. He succeeded [[Richard Nixon]] in August 1974. His presidency was overshadowed by [[Watergate scandal|Watergate]] and recession, and his pardon of Nixon remained controversial. U.S. involvement in the [[Vietnam War]] effectively ended with the [[Fall of Saigon]] during his term. He narrowly lost the 1976 election to [[Jimmy Carter]]. He is the only person to hold both offices without being elected to either.

German visual artist, known for photorealistic and abstract painting, photographs and glass works. Born in [[Dresden]], he trained in socialist realist mural painting at the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts, then left [[East Germany]] for the West in 1961. His 1988 cycle *October 18, 1977* consists of fifteen blurred grisaille paintings based on press images of [[Red Army Faction]] members who died in prison, probing terrorism and media representation. A 2007 window in [[Cologne Cathedral]] comprises 11,500 glass squares in 72 colors, arranged at random to evoke both digital pixels and medieval tradition. His abstract paintings are made by scraping layers of wet paint. Several of his works have set record prices at auction, and he was at one time the most expensive living painter.

Medical specialty focused on the health needs of older adults. Geriatric medicine aims to promote health by preventing, diagnosing and treating disease in older people, who are more likely to have chronic conditions and need more medical care. The term derives from the Greek words "old man" and "healer". Common diseases may present atypically in older patients: [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] may cause low-grade fever and confusion rather than high fever and cough. Geriatric care is interdisciplinary, drawing on [[Medicine|medicine]], [[Nursing|nursing]], pharmacy, social work, and physical and occupational therapy, and covers medication management, memory care, rehabilitation and long-term care. Care is guided by patient goals and preferences rather than a set age. Geriatrics is sometimes called medical gerontology, but it is distinct from gerontology, the multidisciplinary study of [[Ageing|aging]].

Association of 39 mostly German-speaking states in [[Central Europe]] (1815–1866). Created by the [[Congress of Vienna]] to replace the [[Holy Roman Empire]], which dissolved in 1806 as a result of the [[Napoleonic Wars]], it had a single organ, the Federal Convention, presided over by [[Austrian Empire|Austria]] but without a head of state. Most important decisions required unanimity, and its purpose was largely limited to security, making it essentially a military alliance. Its effectiveness depended on cooperation between Austria and [[Prussia]], which often opposed each other. The revolutions of 1848–1849 sought a unified federal state under the Frankfurt Constitution, but the Convention dissolved and was reestablished in 1850 after the revolution was crushed. The Confederation ended after Prussia defeated Austria in the [[Austro-Prussian War]] of 1866. Most historians consider it weak and ineffective; its weakness was part of its design, as the great powers did not want a German nation-state.

German state, also called Imperial Germany or the Second Reich (1871–1918). Founded on January 18, 1871, when the south German states joined the North German Confederation, it was led by the king of [[Prussia]], who was also German emperor. Prussia held about two-thirds of its population and territory. [[Otto von Bismarck]] served as chancellor from 1871 to 1890 and introduced pioneering social programs that laid the foundation for the modern welfare state. By 1913 Germany was the largest economy in continental Europe and the third largest in the world, and one-third of all Nobel Prizes went to German inventors and researchers. Under [[Wilhelm II]], Germany pursued an aggressive course, and in the [[World War I|First World War]] its plans to capture Paris failed. The November 1918 revolution forced Wilhelm II to abdicate and the empire collapsed. The humiliation and economic devastation that followed the [[Treaty of Versailles]] are considered leading factors in the rise of [[Adolf Hitler]] and Nazism.

Medium to large German breed of working dog, known in Britain as the Alsatian. Developed in [[Germany]] from 1899 by Max von Stephanitz, using traditional German herding dogs, the breed was bred for working ability; Stephanitz founded the Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde that year. The breed gained international recognition after [[World War I]]. Originally bred to herd sheep, it has since been used for disability assistance, search-and-rescue, police work and warfare. It is intelligent and obedient, is commonly kept as a companion, and is among the most frequently registered breeds worldwide.

Species of small [[Cockroach|cockroach]], known colloquially as the croton bug. *Blattella germanica* is 1.1 to 1.6 cm long and tan to almost black, with two dark streaks on the pronotum. It is probably the most widely troublesome of the few domestic cockroach pests, occurring on every continent except Antarctica. It is strongly associated with [[Restaurant|restaurants]], [[Hotel|hotels]] and [[Hospital|hospitals]], and as an omnivorous [[Scavenger|scavenger]] it is attracted to meats, starches and sugars. It emits an unpleasant odor when frightened, and it is an intermediate host of the parasite *Moniliformis kalahariensis*.

Literary works written in the German language. Medieval works include the *Hildebrandslied*, the heroic epic *Heliand*, and courtly epics such as the *Nibelungenlied*. [[Martin Luther]]'s Bible translation, published between 1522 and 1534, helped standardize Modern High German. Modern German literature began with Enlightenment authors such as Herder, and Goethe's best-selling *The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) ended the Sensibility movement. [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]] and [[Friedrich Schiller|Schiller]] led the Sturm und Drang and Weimar Classicism movements, and [[Romanticism|German Romanticism]] dominated the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Under the Nazi regime, some authors went into exile and others practiced "internal emigration". German-language authors have won the Nobel Prize in Literature 14 times, including [[Thomas Mann]] and [[Hermann Hesse]].

Process by which East Germany joined the Federal Republic of Germany, from 1989 to 1990. It began with the fall of the [[Berlin Wall]] on November 9, 1989, which followed mass protests by East German citizens and the opening of Hungary's border with Austria earlier that year. The first free elections in the German Democratic Republic were held on March 18, 1990, and a Unification Treaty followed. Reunification took effect on October 3, 1990, when the German Democratic Republic dissolved and its states joined the Federal Republic; East and West [[Berlin]] became a single city, later the capital. The Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany, negotiated with the four occupying powers, granted full sovereignty on March 15, 1991. The reunited state was an enlarged continuation of West Germany, keeping its seats in [[NATO]] and the United Nations and leaving the [[Warsaw Pact]].

Branch of the Indo-European language family. Spoken natively by about 515 million people, mainly in [[Europe]], North America, [[Oceania]] and [[Southern Africa]], the languages all derive from Proto-Germanic, spoken in Iron Age [[Scandinavia]] and northern Germany. The West Germanic branch includes English, the most widely spoken Germanic language with around 360–400 million native speakers; [[Germany|German]] with over 100 million; and Dutch with 24 million. The North Germanic languages Swedish, Danish and Norwegian are partly mutually intelligible, while Icelandic, Faroese and Elfdalian are more conservative. The East Germanic branch, now extinct, included Gothic, Burgundian and Vandalic; Crimean Gothic was spoken until the late 18th century. The family shares the consonant change known as Grimm's law.

Traditional religion of the [[Germanic peoples]]. It spanned at least a thousand years and an area covering Scandinavia, the British Isles, modern Germany and the Netherlands, and its beliefs varied. Few sources were written by pagans themselves; most were written by outsiders, complicating reconstruction. The Germanic peoples believed in many gods and supernatural beings such as giants, dwarfs, elves and dragons. Early medieval sources name the gods [[Odin]], [[Thor]], Tyr and Frigg. Ritual evidence includes rich burials in ships or wagons, wooden figures found in [[Bog|bogs]], and sacrificial deposits in springs and bogs. Sacred sites included groves and temples, and divination, magic and festivals are attested. Germanic religion was influenced by the [[Celts]], the Romans and, later, [[Christianity]].

Tribal groups of Northern Europe in classical antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, including the Roman-era Germani and, most notably, the [[Goths]]. Under [[Augustus|Emperor Augustus]], Rome tried to conquer Germania but withdrew after its defeat at the [[Battle of the Teutoburg Forest]] in 9 CE. During the Migration Period (375–568), Germanic peoples entered the [[Roman Empire]] and founded their own kingdoms. The [[Franks]] became the most powerful, and [[Charlemagne]] claimed the title of Holy Roman Emperor in 800. Scholars debate whether "Germanic peoples" is a valid category, since these groups did not necessarily share an identity.

Grayish-white metalloid, chemical element with symbol Ge and atomic number 32. Germanium is lustrous and hard-brittle, similar in appearance to silicon, and ranks 50th in abundance in Earth's crust. [[Dmitri Mendeleev]] predicted it in 1869 as "ekasilicon". Clemens Winkler discovered it in 1886 in the mineral argyrodite at Freiberg and named it after Germany, his country of birth. It is mined mainly from sphalerite, the primary ore of zinc. Germanium was the basis of the first decade of [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] electronics and was used in [[Transistor|transistors]]. Its major modern uses include fiber-optic systems, infrared optics, [[Solar cell|solar cells]] and [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diodes]]. Synthetic soluble germanium salts are nephrotoxic.

Men's association football team representing Germany. It played its first match in 1908 and is governed by the German Football Association (DFB), founded in 1900. It represents the reunified Federal Republic; separate teams represented [[West Germany]] (1949–1990) and [[East Germany]] (1952–1990). Germany has won four [[FIFA World Cup|FIFA World Cups]] (1954, 1974, 1990 and 2014) and three [[UEFA European Championship|UEFA European Championships]] (1972, 1980 and 1996). It also won the FIFA Confederations Cup in 2017. Germany was the first of only two nations to win both the FIFA World Cup and the [[FIFA Women's World Cup]], the other being Spain.

Italian Renaissance polymath. His interests ranged across mathematics, medicine, astrology, philosophy, music theory and gambling, and he wrote more than 200 works on science. He introduced the [[Binomial theorem|binomial coefficients and binomial theorem]] to the Western world and was a key figure in the foundations of [[Probability|probability]]. In his 1545 book *Ars Magna* he made the first systematic use of [[Negative number|negative numbers]] in Europe, published others' solutions to cubic and quartic equations, and acknowledged [[Imaginary number|imaginary numbers]]. He partly invented the combination lock, the gimbal and the Cardan shaft with universal joints. Cardano practiced medicine in [[Milan]], and in 1570 was imprisoned by the [[Inquisition|Roman Inquisition]] for alleged heresy tied to judicial astrology.

Political manipulation of electoral district boundaries to advantage a party or group. Opposing voters are weakened by "cracking", spreading them across many districts, or "packing", concentrating them in one. The word joins Governor Elbridge Gerry's name with "salamander", after a contorted [[Massachusetts]] district drawn in 1812 for the benefit of the [[Democratic-Republican Party]]. Gerry personally disapproved of the practice. The term carries negative connotations, and gerrymandering is almost always considered a corruption of the democratic process. In *Rucho v. Common Cause* (2019), the U.S. Supreme Court held partisan gerrymandering claims nonjusticiable under federal law.

School of psychology and theory of perception that emphasizes whole patterns. It holds that perception processes entire configurations rather than separate elements, so the whole differs from the sum of its parts. It emerged in the early 20th century in [[Germany]] and [[Austria]] as a rejection of the elementalist and structuralist psychology of [[Wilhelm Wundt]] and Edward Titchener. Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Köhler founded the movement; *Gestalt* means "form" or "pattern". The concept had been introduced in 1890 by Christian von Ehrenfels, who described a melody as having a form-quality that survives transposition to another key. Gestalt psychologists formulated laws of perceptual organization, including proximity, similarity, closure and figure–ground. Several founders emigrated to the United States during the rise of Nazism, which helped spread their ideas in American psychology.

Official secret police of [[Nazi Germany]] and German-occupied Europe. Formed in 1933 as the *Geheime Staatspolizei* (Secret State Police) by [[Hermann Göring]] from Prussia's political police agencies, it came under [[Heinrich Himmler]] of the [[Schutzstaffel|SS]] in 1934. It targeted political opponents, clergy, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals and, above all, Jews, often holding prisoners without judicial process. Though relatively small, it was effective because ordinary Germans reported their fellow citizens. It played a key role in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] and was declared a criminal organization at the [[Nuremberg trials]].

Brazilian military officer, lawyer and politician; president of [[Brazil]] in 1930–1945 and 1951–1954. Vargas took power in the Brazilian Revolution of 1930, which ousted President Washington Luís and ended the oligarchic First Brazilian Republic dominated by [[São Paulo]] and [[Minas Gerais]] elites. He governed provisionally, then was elected under a new constitution in 1934. In 1937 he seized dictatorial powers and established the *Estado Novo*, which curtailed civil liberties and censored the press while pursuing state-led industrialization and labor reforms. In 1942 he took Brazil into World War II on the Allied side, after initial sympathy for the [[Axis powers|Axis]]. Deposed by a military coup in 1945, he returned democratically in 1950, but his second term ended in scandal and his suicide. Historians regard him as the most influential Brazilian politician of the 20th century, though admirers and critics debate his legacy.
